task_description: Implement Taskboard API task attachments and project webhooks: multipart upload of any file type up to 10 MB per file to a task, stored through an AttachmentStorage interface (local filesystem volume in dev, Amazon S3 in AWS) under server-generated keys, listed and downloaded with the original filename; and an outbound webhook notifier that, when a task changes status, POSTs a JSON event to the project's user-configured webhook URL asynchronously from a background thread pool with a short retry.

threats.name: An uploaded archive writes files outside the target folder when extracted
Long-lived storage keys are shipped to the browser or mobile app
One user reads or changes another user's data by changing an id in the request
Storage bucket is publicly listable or readable
Sensitive fields are stored unencrypted, so a backup or database leak exposes them
The server is tricked into fetching internal addresses or cloud metadata
Outbound calls skip certificate checks, so traffic can be intercepted
Attacker uploads a script that your server runs or serves
Attacker uses ../ in a filename to overwrite files
Unvalidated input reaches business logic and breaks assumptions
Queue messages are trusted without checking, so one bad message breaks the worker or the data
An uploaded SVG or HTML file runs script when other users open it
Huge files or compression bombs fill disk or memory
A slow or huge remote response ties up workers and memory
Failing jobs retry forever and starve other work

countermeasures.name: Extract archives safely
countermeasures.how_to: Ignore paths inside archives, reject symlinks and entries that escape the target folder, and cap size and file count.

countermeasures.name: Give clients short-lived, narrowly scoped credentials
countermeasures.how_to: Issue pre-signed or token-exchanged credentials limited to one object or prefix. Never ship long-lived keys to clients.

countermeasures.name: Check the user owns the object on every request
countermeasures.how_to: Look the object up by id AND owner, or check ownership explicitly, and return 404 when they do not match.

countermeasures.name: Keep storage private and hand out short-lived signed URLs
countermeasures.how_to: Block public access on the bucket and issue signed URLs that expire in minutes.

countermeasures.name: Encrypt sensitive data at rest
countermeasures.how_to: Use AES-GCM or your cloud provider's managed encryption, with keys held outside the database.

countermeasures.name: Fetch only allow-listed destinations
countermeasures.how_to: Resolve the host, block private, loopback, and link-local ranges including cloud metadata, and prefer a fixed allow-list of hosts.

countermeasures.name: Do not follow redirects on server-side fetches
countermeasures.how_to: Disable automatic redirects, or re-validate each hop against the same allow-list.

countermeasures.name: Always verify TLS certificates
countermeasures.how_to: Never set verify=False or NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED=0. Add your private CA to the trust store if needed.

countermeasures.name: Allow only the file types you need
countermeasures.how_to: Check the extension and the real file content against an allow-list. Ignore the client's Content-Type.

countermeasures.name: Never use the user's filename or path
countermeasures.how_to: Generate your own filenames, store files outside the web root, and make sure uploads are never executed.

countermeasures.name: Validate all input on the server
countermeasures.how_to: Check type, length, range, and format for every input on the server. Client-side checks are only for convenience.

countermeasures.name: Validate job payloads like any other input
countermeasures.how_to: Check the schema of every queue message and drop or dead-letter anything that does not match.

countermeasures.name: Serve uploads so browsers cannot run them
countermeasures.how_to: Send the correct Content-Type, Content-Disposition attachment for downloads, nosniff, and serve user files from a separate domain.

countermeasures.name: Sanitize user-provided HTML
countermeasures.how_to: Run user HTML through a maintained sanitizer such as DOMPurify or bleach with a strict allow-list. Prefer markdown or plain text.

countermeasures.name: Limit file size and decompressed size
countermeasures.how_to: Set a maximum size per file, and cap decompressed size and file count for archives.

countermeasures.name: Set timeouts and response size caps
countermeasures.how_to: Use connect and read timeouts and a maximum body size on every outbound call and queue consumer.

countermeasures.name: Bound retries with backoff
countermeasures.how_to: Cap retry counts, use exponential backoff, and send failures to a dead-letter queue.

also_consider.name: A user calls an admin or other-role function because only the UI hides it
Sensitive data travels over plain HTTP or an unencrypted connection
Debug features or consoles are left on in production
.env, .git, or backup files are reachable from the web
A request sets fields the user should not control, such as role or price
A user skips or repeats steps in a multi-step flow, such as verification or checkout
Another website makes a logged-in user's browser perform actions
API responses include more fields than the client needs, such as hashes or internal ids

assessment.summary: 15 threats and 17 countermeasures for file-upload, object-storage, outbound-http-request, background-job. Risk level high (highest threat severity).

instructions: Build these countermeasures in as you write the code, starting with the most severe threats. These threats come from the components you picked. also_consider lists general threats from implied components; pass those components explicitly for full detail. After writing code, call general_verify_code_security with the same components.
